title: Aphrodite leaves the battle
intro: Diomedes taunts Aphrodite out of the martial sphere. Apollo takes over Aeneas’ rescue, while Iris escorts the wounded goddess to Ares and then Olympus. The divine characters suffer pain even though they cannot die.

notes.text: τοὔνεκα is crasis of τοῦ ἕνεκα, ‘for that reason.’ ἀναίμων means ‘bloodless,’ qualifying the preceding description of ichor rather than denying the visible fluid. κάββαλεν is an epic assimilated form of κατέβαλεν, aorist of καταβάλλω, ‘dropped.’ ἕο is third-person genitive, ‘from herself.’

μετά with dative gives ‘in / among his hands.’ ἐρύσατο is aorist middle of ἐρύομαι in the protective sense, ‘saved, guarded.’ κυάνεος is dark blue or blue-black, describing the cloud. The following μή clause repeats the danger earlier prevented by Aphrodite’s robe: a Greek might kill Aeneas while he is helpless.

εἶκε is present imperative of εἴκω, ‘give way, withdraw,’ taking the genitives of what she must leave. δηϊοτής means hostile fighting or battle. θύγατερ is the vocative of θυγάτηρ. Diomedes addresses Zeus’ daughter directly and authoritatively, making his divine permission sound like personal dominance.

ἅλις is ‘enough’; ὅττι introduces what is enough for her, deceiving women. ἠπεροπεύω means ‘beguile, deceive.’ πωλήσεαι is an epic second-singular form of πωλέομαι, ‘frequent, come and go,’ not πωλέω, ‘sell.’ ῥιγήσειν is future infinitive of ῥιγέω, ‘shudder at,’ after ὀΐω.

πύθηαι is epic second-singular aorist middle subjunctive of πυνθάνομαι, ‘hear, learn’: she will fear battle even when hearing of it elsewhere. ἀλύουσα, from ἀλύω, describes distress or bewilderment. ποδήνεμος, ‘wind-footed,’ characterizes Iris. ἑλοῦσα is aorist active participle of αἱρέω, ‘taking hold of her.’

ὀδύνῃσι is epic dative plural of ὀδύνη, pain. χρόα is accusative of χρώς, her skin, marking the respect in which she darkens or discolours. ἥμενον is present participle of ἧμαι, ‘sit.’ ἐκέκλιτο is pluperfect middle/passive of κλίνω, ‘was resting / leaning’; ἠέρι is dative of ἀήρ, here mist. Ares remains where Athena had left him.

ἐριποῦσα is aorist participle of ἐρείπω, ‘fall,’ with γνύξ, ‘on the knees.’ κασίγνητος means brother or close sibling. λίσσομαι is the verb of earnest supplication. ᾔτεεν is uncontracted imperfect of αἰτέω, ‘asked for.’ χρυσάμπυκας describes the horses’ gold headbands or frontlets.

κόμισαι is aorist middle imperative of κομίζω, ‘take care of / convey me.’ δός is aorist imperative of δίδωμι. ἵκωμαι is first-singular aorist middle subjunctive of ἱκνέομαι after purpose ὄφρα. ἕδος is a seat or abode; Olympus is the gods’ dwelling.

notes.lemma: ἄχθομαι ἕλκος · καὶ ἂν Διὶ … μάχοιτο
notes.text: ἕλκος is accusative of the thing causing distress, ‘I suffer terribly from the wound.’ The relative ὅ continues the wound as the object of οὔτασεν. καί intensifies the potential claim: Diomedes ‘would fight even father Zeus.’ μάχοιτο is present middle optative with ἄν, and Διί is the dative opponent. This is Aphrodite’s aggrieved exaggeration.

ἀκηχεμένη is perfect middle/passive participle of ἀκαχίζω, ‘grieved,’ with accusative of respect φίλον ἦτορ, ‘in her heart.’ λάζετο is imperfect of λάζομαι, ‘took hold of,’ with reins as object. Iris stands beside Aphrodite and assumes the driver’s role.

ἐλάαν is epic infinitive of ἐλαύνω, ‘drive,’ after the whipping action. πετέσθην is third-dual aorist middle of πέτομαι, ‘flew’; τώ and ἀέκοντε are dual, ‘the two, not unwilling.’ ἔστησε is transitive aorist of ἵστημι, ‘stopped,’ unlike intransitive ἔστη, ‘stood.’ Iris brings the team to rest at Olympus.
